Warehouse Purpose

OLTP Workload

OLAP Workload

Row Storage

OLTP stores whole rows together

Column Storage

OLAP stores whole columns together: same table, different layout

Rows and Columns on Disk

Twelve values, two orders on disk

When Each Layout Wins

One row: row store wins. One column over all rows: column store wins

IndexA sorted copy of one column, pointing back at the rows

Without an index, WHERE machine = 'M17' reads every row: a full scan.
An index on machine is a separate structure, sorted by that column, that lists the rows holding each value. The database searches it like a dictionary (a B-tree: log n steps) and reads only those rows.
Lecture 6’s optimizer slide chose between “scan” and “use the index”. This is the index it meant.
CREATE INDEX idx_machine
    ON events(machine);
idx_machine (sorted)
machinerowids
M0112, 57, 91, …
M023, 48, …
……
M177, 30, 66, …
……
Sorted by the indexed column, pointing back at the rows: a dictionary for one column

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE machine = 'M17';
detail
SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx (machine=?)
The plan changes from SCAN events to SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx. An aggregate over every row (AVG(temp)) still scans: an index speeds up finding rows, not reading all of them.
SCAN becomes SEARCH … USING INDEX; an aggregate over all rows still scans

Column CompressionSorted columns repeat, and repeats compress

A column holds one type; sorted, equal values sit together. Two encodings use that:
  • Run-length encoding: (value, count)
    • A A A A B B C → (A,4) (B,2) (C,1)
  • Dictionary encoding: distinct strings become small integers
    • India, Germany, US → 0, 1, 2 + a dictionary
So the sort order sets the file size: long runs come from sorting on the low-cardinality column. Parquet and Capacitor do this per column.
Country (sorted)RLE
India(India, 2)
India
Germany(Germany, 1)
US(US, 1)
One type per column and equal values adjacent: the sort order sets the file size

Star Schema QueryJoin the fact table to the dimensions this query needs, then aggregate

SELECT   month, category, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM     fact_sales
JOIN     dim_date    USING (date_key)
JOIN     dim_product USING (product_key)
GROUP BY month, category
ORDER BY month, total DESC;
monthcategorytotal
2025-01Snack2000
2025-01Frozen800
2025-01Meal300
2025-02Snack2500
2025-02Dessert1800
2025-02Meal200
Join the dimensions needed for grouping or filtering, then aggregate the measures

Recap: Data Warehouse

Structured in, structured out: the warehouse holds tables only

Data Lake

Everything in its native shape, transformed later, if at all

Difference Between Data Storages

Scope, type, schema timing, use: schema on write vs schema on read is the hinge

Data Lake → Warehouse

ETL (extract, transform, load): transform before the destination, on a separate engine. ELT (extract, load, transform): load raw, then transform inside the destination, usually as SQL (dbt is the common tool). The difference is where the T runs.
Lake and warehouse stand apart; the T between them runs outside (ETL) or inside (ELT) the destination

Lakehouse Storage and Queries

Lake storage underneath, warehouse behaviour on top: one system

Warehouse, lake, lakehouse: the third puts a metadata layer on the lake

Lakehouse Internals

1Storage layer: add transactions, versioning & more
2New query engine designs: great SQL performance on data lake storage systems and file formats
3Optimized access for data science & ML

Open Table Formats

Adds to plain Parquet filesWhat it means in practice
Transactionsatomic commits; conflicting writers may retry or fail
Schema evolutionadd or rename a column without rewriting the files
Time travelquery or restore retained snapshots; retention limits history
Engine interoperabilityread/write support depends on format, version and catalog
Iceberg and Delta Lake turn a folder of Parquet files into a table

Case study: Netflix’s Iceberg TablesNetflix’s legacy Hive tables had no table-wide commit, so Iceberg tracks files in metadata

An atomic metadata commit switches readers from one complete snapshot to another

Abstraction = Hiding Complexity

Above the water an API; below it, everything this lecture described

Data Orchestration

Data orchestration is the process of taking siloed data from multiple data storage locations, combining and organizing it, and making it available for data analysis tools. It can also include tasks like provisioning resources and monitoring.
Data Pipelines, Workflows, Jobs
cron   a crontab line cannot express “run B after A succeeds, retry twice, alert me”

Data Pipeline

Source, ingest, store, transform, publish, consume: the course in one row

The Tool Should

  • Define tasks and their dependencies
    • start, branch, parallel, loop, skip, condition, end
  • Trigger them
    • on a schedule, on an event, on a dependency, ad hoc
  • Let you act via UI, API, CLI
    • create, start, stop, pause, resume, delete
  • Show what happened
    • visualization, metrics, alerts, notification, admin
  • Integrate with everything
    • databases, warehouses, lakes, file stores, compute, APIs
+ run anywhere, be available, scalable, reliable, secure, and cheap
That tool is a workflow orchestrator. The most used one is Apache Airflow.

Airflow: Architecture

DAG files in, scheduler decides, workers run, metadata DB remembers

Airflow DAG

Workflows are called DAGs for Directed Acyclic Graph.

Airflow Tasks

  • Tasks: A task is an instance of an operator, or a decorated Python function.
  • Tasks can execute work or submit jobs to external systems.
  • We tend to classify operators in 3 categories: Sensors, Operators, Transfers.

Airflow: Code Example

from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.empty import EmptyOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

with DAG("file_sensor_example",
         start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
         schedule="*/5 * * * *", catchup=False,
         default_args={"retries": 1, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}) as dag:
    start = EmptyOperator(task_id="start")
    wait = FileSensor(task_id="wait_for_file", fs_conn_id="fs_default",
                      filepath="input.csv", mode="reschedule",
                      poke_interval=30, timeout=600)
    stop = EmptyOperator(task_id="stop")
    start >> wait >> stop
Airflow 3.x + standard provider; configure fs_default with the watched folder.

Airflow: Monitoring DAG Status

Historical Airflow UI: run states, schedule and concurrency

Airflow: Common Pattern

Input form, a DAG of processing, output dashboard: people see only the ends

dbt: Transformations as SQL Files

-- models/daily_sales.sql
SELECT order_date, region, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
GROUP BY order_date, region
$ dbt run     # builds every model, in dependency order
$ dbt build   # builds and tests in DAG order; errors block descendants
Each SQL model is one SELECT; ref() tells dbt the order to build them

Data Quality Checks

# models/schema.yml
models:
  - name: daily_sales
    columns:
      - name: order_date
        data_tests: [not_null]
      - name: region
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments:
                values: ['Asia', 'Europe', 'Americas']
A pipeline that finished is not a pipeline that is right; write the checks down

When a Run Fails

ProblemWhat to doIn Airflow
A task hits a flaky networktry again a few timesretries=3, retry_delay
Yesterday’s run never happenedrun it for that date laterbackfill, catchup
A rerun would double the rowsmake the task idempotentoverwrite the date partition
Plan for failure: retry, backfill, and make every rerun idempotent

Caveat: Non-Idempotent LoadRetrying the append duplicates October 3 and doubles that day’s reported sales

INSERT INTO daily_sales           -- the 10-03 run
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) FROM raw_orders
WHERE order_date = '2025-10-03'
GROUP BY order_date;
INSERT INTO daily_sales           -- retried
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) FROM raw_orders
WHERE order_date = '2025-10-03'
GROUP BY order_date;
SELECT * FROM daily_sales;
order_datetotal
2025-10-02500
2025-10-03500
2025-10-03500
Remedy: atomically replace the date partition, or MERGE one source row per key
Same day, two rows: October 3 now reports double

Lineage: Which Table Came From Which

Follow the edges back to find the cause, forward to find what to rebuild

Takeaway: Big Data II

1Design the grain and dimension history; column storage reduces analytical I/O
2Choose warehouse or lakehouse by workload and cost; ELT and open table formats organize stored data
3Airflow schedules the steps and dbt builds SQL models; test data, make reruns idempotent, and track lineage
